w:r.w:t: Bloom
Reproductive Health Tracking Platform
Final Documentation — Jahzara’s Sections
2.1 Frontend Technologies

The Bloom platform is built on a web-based frontend architecture carefully selected to maximise accessibility, responsiveness, and ease of use across a wide range of devices and screen sizes. Every technology decision was driven by the goal of delivering a lightweight yet powerful interface that non-technical users — particularly those managing their reproductive health for the first time — can navigate with confidence.
Core Technologies
The three foundational web technologies underpin the entire Bloom user interface:
HTML5

HyperText Markup Language (HTML5) forms the structural backbone of all Bloom pages. Semantic HTML elements are used throughout — including <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, and <footer> — to create a logical document outline that benefits both screen readers and search engines. Custom data attributes (data-*) are used extensively to attach cycle metadata to DOM elements without polluting the JavaScript layer with direct DOM queries.
CSS3

Cascading Style Sheets handle all presentation and layout concerns. Bloom uses a structured, modular CSS architecture built around the Bloom Design System — a set of reusable design tokens and component rules. Key CSS3 features in use include:
CSS Custom Properties (variables) for the global colour palette, spacing scale, and typography scale — enabling a single source of truth that propagates across every page.
Flexbox and CSS Grid for responsive, multi-column layouts that reflow gracefully on mobile, tablet, and desktop viewports.
Media queries with breakpoints at 480 px, 768 px, and 1200 px to guarantee that the dashboard, calendar, resource centre, and clinic finder are each fully usable on any screen size.

CSS transitions and keyframe animations for micro-interactions such as modal slide-in, card hover lifts, and loading spinners — providing visual feedback that the application is responding to the user.
A pink-centred colour palette anchored on the Bloom primary colour (#C2187A), supported by light tints, neutrals, and accessible contrast ratios meeting WCAG 2.1 AA requirements for text legibility.
JavaScript (ES6+)

JavaScript is the dynamic engine of the frontend. Modern ES6+ syntax — including arrow functions, destructuring, template literals, async/await, and ES modules — is used throughout to keep the codebase readable and maintainable. JavaScript responsibilities in Bloom are divided into three broad areas:
Dynamic content rendering:
Cycle phase cards and prediction banners on the Dashboard are generated in real time from Firestore data.
Calendar overlays — highlighting predicted period days, fertile windows, and ovulation estimates — are painted onto the monthly grid each time the user navigates to a new month.
The Resource Centre dynamically injects educational pamphlet cards from the database, applying category filters and search results without a page reload.
User interaction handling:
The Cycle Log Modal captures multi-field input (flow intensity, symptoms, sleep score, stress level, activity level, and notes) and validates each field before submitting the payload to Firestore.
Clinic Finder filter controls (parish, clinic type, service type) bind to the map and card list simultaneously, updating both views in real time.
A "Use My Location" button triggers the browser Geolocation API, re-centres the Leaflet map, and re-ranks clinic cards by proximity.
Firebase data binding:
Authentication state changes (sign-in, sign-out, session expiry) are observed via Firebase Auth onAuthStateChanged listeners, which gate access to all protected pages.
Firestore real-time listeners update the Dashboard and Calendar automatically whenever a new cycle log is written, so the user always sees the latest data without refreshing.
Design System
The Bloom Design System enforces visual consistency across every page. Its key principles are:

Component-Based Architecture

The frontend is organised as a collection of modular, reusable UI components. Each component owns its own HTML structure, CSS rules, and JavaScript event handlers, making it easy to maintain, test, and reuse across pages. The primary components are:
Cycle Snapshot Card — displays current cycle day, phase label, and a progress ring.
Cycle Phase Card — provides a human-friendly description of the current menstrual phase (menstruation, follicular, ovulation, luteal) with colour coding.
Cycle Log Modal — a focus-trapped overlay for data entry, dismissible via keyboard (Esc) or backdrop click.
Resource Cards — thumbnail-plus-text cards rendered from a Firestore collection, supporting category badges and estimated read times.
Clinic Cards — information cards combining clinic name, services offered, parish, contact number, and action buttons (Get Directions, View on Map).
External Libraries
Where native browser APIs are insufficient, carefully chosen third-party libraries extend the frontend:

Leaflet.js (v1.9) — an open-source mapping library used for the interactive clinic map. Leaflet renders OpenStreetMap tiles, places custom pin markers for each clinic, and supports pan/zoom interactions on both desktop and mobile.
OpenStreetMap — provides the free, open-licence tile layer rendered inside Leaflet, eliminating the need for a paid mapping API.
2.4 APIs & External Services (Frontend)

The Bloom frontend integrates with a suite of external services to deliver real-time data, secure authentication, interactive mapping, and location-aware features. All integrations are managed through asynchronous JavaScript, ensuring that network operations never block the main UI thread.
Firebase Authentication
Firebase Authentication manages every aspect of user identity in Bloom.
Registration: New users create an account with an email address and password. The Firebase SDK hashes and stores credentials securely; Bloom never touches raw passwords.
Login: Returning users authenticate with their credentials. Upon success, Firebase issues a JSON Web Token (JWT) that Bloom stores in memory and attaches to all Firestore requests.
Session persistence: Firebase Auth persists the session across browser tabs and page refreshes using IndexedDB, so users remain logged in for a configurable session window.

Auth state listener: The onAuthStateChanged observer fires on every page load. If no valid session exists, the user is redirected to the login screen; if a session is found, the protected page renders normally.
Sign-out: Calling firebase.auth().signOut() invalidates the local token and redirects to the landing page.
Firebase Firestore
Cloud Firestore is the primary database for all user-generated and application data. Bloom uses the following collection structure:

Firestore security rules restrict reads and writes to the authenticated owner of each document, ensuring no user can access another user’s cycle data.
Leaflet.js + OpenStreetMap
The Clinic Finder’s interactive map is powered by Leaflet.js rendering OpenStreetMap tiles.
On page load, Leaflet initialises a map centred on Jamaica (lat 18.1096, lng −77.2975, zoom 9).
Clinic coordinates from Firestore are converted into Leaflet markers with custom pink pin icons matching the Bloom brand.
Clicking a marker opens a Leaflet popup displaying the clinic name, parish, and a “View Details” link that scrolls to the corresponding clinic card.
The map is fully touch-enabled, supporting pinch-zoom and drag-pan on mobile devices.
Geolocation API (Routing / Location Services)
The “Use My Location” feature leverages the browser’s native Geolocation API:
When the user clicks the button, navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition() requests permission and returns the device’s GPS coordinates.
Bloom re-centres the Leaflet map on the user’s position and adds a distinct “You are here” marker.
Clinic cards are re-sorted by Haversine distance so that the nearest clinics appear at the top of the list.
The “Get Directions” button constructs a Google Maps deep-link URL using the user’s coordinates and the clinic’s coordinates, opening turn-by-turn navigation in a new browser tab.
3.6.1 External Interfaces — User Interface

The Bloom user interface is the primary point of interaction between the user and the system. It is designed to present complex menstrual health data in a clear, reassuring, and visually consistent way. Each interface is responsive and tested across Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge on both desktop and mobile viewports.
Dashboard
The Dashboard is the first screen a user sees after logging in. It provides an at-a-glance summary of the user’s current cycle state and recent health trends.

Cycle Snapshot Card: Shows the current cycle day (e.g., “Day 14”), the cycle phase name, and a circular progress ring that fills as the cycle progresses. A coloured arc segment indicates whether the user is in the menstruation, follicular, ovulation, or luteal phase.

Cycle Phase Card: Provides a short, plain-English description of the current phase, its typical duration, and associated symptoms or mood patterns, helping users understand what to expect from their body.
Next Period Banner: Displays the predicted start date of the next period, calculated using the user’s historical average cycle length stored in Firestore.
Trend Charts: Line and bar charts (rendered via Chart.js or SVG) display historical data such as average cycle length, symptom frequency, sleep scores, and stress levels across the last 3–12 cycles.
Goal Tool Card: Allows the user to set a personal health focus (e.g., “Improve sleep”, “Reduce stress”) and tracks progress with a simple progress indicator.
Insights Panel: Automatically generated tips and observations (e.g., “Your cycle has been consistently 28 days over the last 4 months”) to educate and motivate the user.
Calendar Interface
The Calendar Interface gives users a month-by-month view of their cycle, combining historical log data with forward-looking predictions.
Monthly Grid: A standard calendar grid where each day cell is colour-coded: red for period days, purple for the fertile window, green for predicted ovulation, and neutral for non-flagged days.
Navigation Controls: Forward and back arrows let users navigate between months. The current day is always highlighted with a pink ring.
Cycle Overlay Panel: A collapsible sidebar or bottom sheet displaying the legend and prediction confidence level for the currently displayed month.
Log Entry Points: Tapping or clicking any day cell that has a log opens a read-only summary of that day’s entry. Clicking today’s cell (or using the floating “+” button) opens the Cycle Log Modal.
Cycle Log Modal
The Cycle Log Modal is the data-entry hub of Bloom. It is a focus-trapped overlay that slides up from the bottom on mobile or appears centred on desktop.
Flow Intensity: A segmented control offering None / Light / Medium / Heavy / Spotting options, colour-coded from light pink to deep red.
Symptoms: A multi-select chip grid covering common symptoms (cramps, bloating, headache, fatigue, mood swings, acne, back pain, breast tenderness, nausea, and a free-text “Other” field).
Biometrics: Numeric sliders for Sleep Score (0–10), Stress Level (0–10), and Activity Level (0–10), each with labelled endpoints for clarity.
Notes: A free-text textarea with a 500-character limit and a live character counter.
Date Selector: Defaults to today but allows the user to back-log entries for up to 7 previous days.
Submit / Cancel Buttons: Submission triggers a Firestore write, closes the modal, and updates the calendar overlay immediately via the real-time listener.
Resource Centre
The Resource Centre provides curated, medically accurate educational content on reproductive health.

Card Grid Layout: Educational pamphlets are displayed as cards in a responsive 1–2–3 column grid depending on screen width. Each card shows a thumbnail image, title, category badge, and estimated read time.
Category Filter Bar: Tabs or chips let users filter content by topic (e.g., Cycle Basics, Nutrition, Contraception, STIs, Mental Health). Selecting a category instantly hides non-matching cards.
Search Bar: A real-time text search filters card titles and descriptions as the user types, with no page reload required.
Reading View: Clicking a card expands it into a full reading view (or opens a modal) with the complete pamphlet content, formatted with headings and bullet lists for easy scanning.
Clinic Finder
The Clinic Finder helps users locate reproductive health clinics across Jamaica.
Search Input: Users can search by clinic name, service offered, or keyword. Results update the map and card list simultaneously.

Filter Controls: Dropdown menus allow filtering by Parish (all 14 parishes), Clinic Type (public health centre, private clinic, NGO), and Service Type (family planning, prenatal care, STI testing, etc.).
Map View: An interactive Leaflet map displays pin markers for all matching clinics. Markers are clustered at low zoom levels to avoid clutter.

Clinic Cards: Below the map, a scrollable list of clinic cards shows the clinic name, parish, phone number, opening hours, and a list of services offered. Each card has “Get Directions” and “View on Map” action buttons.
Use My Location: A GPS button re-centres the map on the user’s device position and re-sorts clinic cards by proximity.
4.4 Usability & Accessibility

Bloom is built on the principle that reproductive health tools should be usable by everyone, regardless of technical ability, device type, or physical capability. The following usability and accessibility features are implemented across all screens.
Usability Features
Navigation

A persistent top navigation bar appears on every page of the authenticated application. It contains the Bloom logo (links to the Dashboard), and labelled navigation items for Calendar, Resources, and Clinic Finder. The active page link is underlined and highlighted in Bloom pink so users always know where they are in the application. On mobile, the navigation collapses into a hamburger menu that slides in from the left, maintaining full functionality on small screens.
Consistent Layout & Visual Structure

All four main pages (Dashboard, Calendar, Resources, Clinic Finder) share the same layout skeleton: a top navigation bar, a page heading with a short description, and a content area below. This consistency means users build a mental model quickly and can switch between features without reorientation. Colour coding is consistent throughout: pink always signals the current cycle phase or a primary action, green signals ovulation, and purple signals the fertile window.
Card-Based UI

Information is chunked into discrete cards rather than presented as walls of text. Each card has a clear heading, a short description, and one or two action buttons. This format mirrors the reading patterns of mobile users and reduces cognitive load by presenting one idea per card. Cards are touch-target sized (minimum 44 × 44 px) for comfortable tapping.
Minimal Input Friction

The Cycle Log Modal is designed to be completable in under 60 seconds. Flow intensity and symptoms use tap-to-select chip controls rather than text fields. Biometric scores use sliders with tactile drag handles. The modal remembers the last-used date and defaults to today, eliminating repetitive date selection. Required fields are minimal: only flow intensity is required; all other fields are optional.
Accessibility Considerations
Colour Contrast

All text and interactive elements meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA contrast requirements. The primary Bloom pink (#C2187A) on a white background achieves a contrast ratio of 5.4:1, exceeding the 4.5:1 minimum for normal text. Dark text (#1A1A1A) on light backgrounds achieves ratios above 15:1. Phase colour-coding is never used as the sole differentiator — each phase also carries a text label and icon to support users with colour-vision deficiencies.
Clear Language

Medical terminology is either avoided or accompanied by a plain-English explanation. For example, “luteual phase” is presented as “Luteal Phase (days after ovulation)”. Tooltips and info icons provide additional context where brevity requires condensed labels. Error messages are written in first person and explain what happened and what to do next (e.g., “We couldn’t save your log. Please check your connection and try again.”).
Large Clickable Areas

Every interactive element — buttons, navigation links, calendar day cells, filter chips, map markers, and card action buttons — has a minimum touch target of 44 × 44 px as recommended by Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines and Google’s Material Design. Adequate spacing between targets prevents accidental mis-taps on mobile.
Structured Content

Semantic HTML heading hierarchy (h1 → h2 → h3) is maintained throughout the application so that screen reader users can navigate by heading. ARIA labels are added to icon-only buttons (e.g., aria-label="Close modal"). Form inputs are associated with visible <label> elements, and all images carry descriptive alt text. The Cycle Log Modal is fully keyboard-navigable, with tab order flowing logically through fields and focus returning to the trigger button on close.
5.5.1 System Decomposition — Frontend

The Bloom frontend is decomposed into four functional modules, each encapsulating a distinct feature area. Within each module, individual UI components handle specific rendering and interaction responsibilities. This modular architecture promotes separation of concerns, reduces the risk of cross-feature regressions, and makes it straightforward to extend or replace individual components without affecting the rest of the application.
Module 1: Dashboard Components
The Dashboard module is responsible for aggregating and displaying the user’s cycle summary on first login.

Cycle Snapshot Card: Fetches the user’s most recent cycle log from Firestore, calculates the current cycle day and phase, and renders a circular progress ring using SVG. Updates in real time via a Firestore onSnapshot listener.

Cycle Phase Card: Maps the current phase enum (MENSTRUATION | FOLLICULAR | OVULATION | LUTEAL) to a human-readable description, phase colour, and a set of typical symptoms. Renders as a colour-bordered card with an icon.
Goal Tool Card: Reads the user’s goal from the users Firestore document, displays a progress bar, and provides an edit button that opens an inline form. Writes goal updates back to Firestore on save.

Insights Panel: Executes a set of client-side analysis functions against the last 6 months of cycle logs to generate plain-English insight strings. Displays up to 3 insights in a collapsible accordion.

Trend Charts: Uses the Chart.js library to render line charts (cycle length over time) and bar charts (average symptom frequency). Data is fetched once on mount and cached in module-level state for the session.
Module 2: Calendar Module
The Calendar module combines historical data with forward-looking cycle predictions in a monthly grid view.

Monthly Calendar View: Generates a 5-or-6-row × 7-column grid from the current month’s date range. Each cell is a <div> with a data-date attribute. Cycle log data and predictions are overlaid by adding CSS classes (period-day, fertile-window, ovulation-day) to the corresponding cells.

Cycle Overlay Panel: A sidebar panel that displays the colour legend, the predicted start and end dates of the next period, and the fertile window range. Values are recalculated whenever the user navigates to a different month.

Cycle Log Modal: (Shared component, instantiated from the Calendar module.) Opening it from the calendar pre-populates the date field with the clicked cell’s date. Submitting a log triggers a Firestore write and immediately re-applies the calendar overlays.
Module 3: Resource Module
The Resource module presents educational content in a filterable, searchable card grid.

Resource Cards: Each card is built from a Firestore resource document. The card template renders a thumbnail, category badge, title, short excerpt, and read-time estimate. Cards are injected into a CSS Grid container via a JavaScript template function.

Category Filters: A horizontal scrollable row of chip buttons. Each chip has a data-category attribute. Clicking a chip calls filterCards(category), which shows/hides cards by matching their data-category attribute. An “All” chip clears the filter.

Search Bar: An <input type="search"> element listens to the input event. On each keystroke, a client-side search function compares the query against card title and excerpt text, showing only matching cards. The search is combined with the active category filter so both constraints apply simultaneously.
Module 4: Clinic Finder Module
The Clinic Finder module combines server data, a mapping library, and location services to help users find nearby clinics.

Filter Controls: Three <select> dropdowns for Parish, Clinic Type, and Service Type. A change event on any dropdown calls applyFilters(), which re-queries the in-memory clinic array and updates both the map markers and the clinic card list.

Map View: Initialised with Leaflet.map(). Clinic coordinates loaded from Firestore are converted to L.marker() instances. Custom Bloom-styled icons (pink map pins) replace Leaflet’s default markers. A L.markerClusterGroup() plugin groups nearby pins at lower zoom levels. Clicking a marker fires a custom event that scrolls the card list to the corresponding clinic card and highlights it.

Clinic Cards: A scrollable <div> column rendered from the filtered clinic array. Each card contains: clinic name (bold heading), parish (sub-heading), services list (chips), phone number (tel: link), and two action buttons. The “Get Directions” button opens a Google Maps URL; the “View on Map” button calls map.flyTo() to centre the Leaflet map on that clinic’s coordinates.
5.7.1 System Interfaces & APIs — Frontend

The Bloom frontend communicates with backend services exclusively through asynchronous JavaScript API calls. No synchronous XMLHttpRequest calls are used; all network operations return Promises or use async/await, ensuring the UI thread remains responsive during data fetching.
Authentication Interface
All authentication operations are routed through the Firebase Authentication SDK:
firebase.auth().createUserWithEmailAndPassword(email, password) — called on the registration form submit. On success, a new Firestore users document is created with the returned uid.

firebase.auth().signInWithEmailAndPassword(email, password) — called on the login form submit. On failure, the SDK returns an error code (e.g., auth/wrong-password) that is mapped to a user-friendly message.
firebase.auth().onAuthStateChanged(callback) — registered on every protected page. The callback is fired once on page load with either a User object (authenticated) or null (unauthenticated).
firebase.auth().signOut() — called when the user clicks the sign-out button. Clears the local session and redirects to the landing page.
Cycle Data Interface
Cycle logs are stored in and retrieved from the cycleLogs Firestore collection:
Fetching: db.collection('cycleLogs').where('uid', '==', currentUser.uid).orderBy('date', 'desc').get() retrieves all logs for the authenticated user, sorted most-recent-first.
Real-time updates: db.collection('cycleLogs').where('uid', '==', uid).onSnapshot(callback) keeps the Dashboard and Calendar in sync without polling.
Writing: db.collection('cycleLogs').add(logObject) creates a new log document. If a log for the selected date already exists, the document is merged using .set(logObject, { merge: true }).

Cycle prediction: Predictions are computed client-side using the last 6 average cycle lengths stored in Firestore, applying a rolling average algorithm. No separate prediction API endpoint is required.
Educational Resources Interface
Resource pamphlets are stored in the resources Firestore collection and fetched once per session:
db.collection('resources').get() retrieves the full resource catalogue on Resource Centre mount. Results are cached in a module-level JavaScript array.
Client-side filtering and search operate against the cached array, eliminating round-trips to Firestore for each filter or search action.
Clinic Data Interface
Clinic records are loaded from the clinics Firestore collection:

db.collection('clinics').get() fetches all clinic documents on Clinic Finder mount. Coordinates, name, parish, services, and contact details are extracted from each document and stored in a local array.
Leaflet markers are created from the local array, so map interactions do not require additional Firestore reads.

The Geolocation API (navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition) is called only when the user explicitly clicks “Use My Location”, respecting user privacy by not requesting location permission automatically on page load.
8.1 Frontend Implementation

The Bloom frontend implementation translates the design system and component architecture into a functioning, production-ready user interface. This section documents the key implemented features, the event-driven interaction model, and the techniques used to keep the UI performant and maintainable.
Dynamic Dashboard

On authenticated page load, the Dashboard executes a Promise.all() that simultaneously fetches the user profile, the most recent 12 cycle logs, and the user’s goal from Firestore. Once all three requests resolve, the Dashboard renders synchronously from the fetched data:
The Cycle Snapshot Card’s progress ring SVG stroke-dashoffset is set proportionally to the ratio of elapsed cycle days to average cycle length.
Phase colour classes (phase-menstruation, phase-follicular, phase-ovulation, phase-luteal) are applied to the Cycle Phase Card container, changing its border and background tint.
Trend charts are drawn by passing the cycle log array to a buildCharts(logs) helper that extracts the relevant metric time series and invokes Chart.js.
A Firestore onSnapshot listener is registered after the initial render, so any new log added from the Calendar page is automatically reflected on the Dashboard within milliseconds.
Interactive Calendar with Prediction Overlays
The calendar grid is generated by a buildCalendar(year, month) function that creates a 2D array of date objects and renders them as a table of <div> cells. Overlay application works in three passes:
Historical pass: Each cycle log document is checked against the cell’s date. If a log exists for that date with non-zero flow, the cell receives the period-day class.

Prediction pass: The rolling average cycle length is used to project the next 3 period start dates and their durations. Projected period cells receive the predicted-period class (lighter shade) to visually distinguish predictions from confirmed logs.
Fertile/ovulation pass: Ovulation is estimated as 14 days before the next predicted period. The 5-day fertile window centred on ovulation day receives the fertile-window class.
Month navigation calls buildCalendar() with the new month parameters and re-applies all three overlay passes against the same data, which is cached from the initial fetch.
Cycle Logging System
The Cycle Log Modal is built as a self-contained component with its own state object (currentLog) that accumulates field values as the user interacts:
Chip selections toggle their active state and push/pop values from currentLog.symptoms[].
Slider inputs update currentLog.sleep, currentLog.stress, or currentLog.activity on every input event, providing live numeric feedback.
On submit, the component validates that flow intensity is selected (the only required field), then calls db.collection('cycleLogs').set(currentLog, { merge: true }) with the date as the document ID.
A loading spinner replaces the submit button during the async write, and a success toast notification is shown on resolution.
Educational Resource Browsing

The Resource Centre uses a virtualised rendering approach for performance: only the cards currently visible in the viewport (plus a small buffer above and below) are fully rendered. As the user scrolls, off-screen cards are replaced with lightweight placeholder divs of the same height. This technique ensures smooth scrolling even with a large resource catalogue.
Clinic Finder with Map Integration
The Clinic Finder feature is initialised in three sequential steps to prevent map rendering errors:
Data load: All clinic documents are fetched from Firestore and stored in a local clinics[] array.

Map initialisation: Leaflet.map() is called on a <div id="map"> container only after the DOM has fully rendered (deferred via requestAnimationFrame to avoid the Leaflet “map container not found” error common when initialising inside conditionally rendered elements).
Marker placement: Clinic coordinates are iterated and L.marker([lat, lng]).addTo(map) is called for each, grouping markers into a cluster layer.

Filter and search operations update the clinics displayed by hiding/showing markers on the map (via layer.setStyle or addTo/removeFrom the cluster group) and re-rendering the card list from the filtered array.
8.4 Clinic Finder

The Clinic Finder is one of Bloom’s most socially impactful features, addressing a documented barrier to reproductive healthcare in Jamaica: many users do not know which clinics in their area offer the specific services they need. By combining a searchable database, a live map, and location services, the Clinic Finder reduces this information gap and makes it significantly easier for users to connect with healthcare providers.
Search Functionality
The search input at the top of the Clinic Finder page accepts free-text queries and filters clinics in real time. The search function compares the query string (lowercased) against:
The clinic’s name field.
The clinic’s services array (each service is individually compared).
The clinic’s parish name.
Results meeting any of these criteria (OR logic) are displayed. The map and card list update simultaneously, ensuring the two views always reflect the same filtered dataset.
Filtering by Parish, Clinic Type, and Services
Three dropdown filter controls provide structured narrowing of the clinic list:
Filter
Options
Behaviour
Parish
All + 14 Jamaican parishes
Shows only clinics in the selected parish
Clinic Type
All, Public Health Centre, Private Clinic, NGO
Filters by the clinic’s type field
Service Type
Family Planning, Prenatal Care, STI Testing, Contraception, and more
Shows clinics that include the selected service in their services[] array

All three filters are applied simultaneously (AND logic), so selecting “St. Andrew” and “STI Testing” shows only clinics in St. Andrew that offer STI testing. Resetting any filter to “All” removes that constraint.
Interactive Map
The Leaflet map provides spatial context that a list alone cannot offer:
Custom pink map-pin icons (SVG, 32 × 40 px) replace Leaflet’s default blue markers, maintaining brand consistency.
Marker clustering groups pins that are within 40 px of each other at the current zoom level into a numbered cluster bubble. Clicking a cluster zooms in to reveal the individual pins.
Clicking an individual marker opens a Leaflet popup with the clinic name and a “View Card” button that smooth-scrolls to the corresponding clinic card below the map and applies a highlight animation.
The map dynamically pans and zooms to fit the bounding box of all filtered markers when a filter or search is applied, so the user always sees all results without manual navigation.
Clinic Cards
Each clinic card presents a structured summary of one clinic:
Header: Clinic name (bold, pink) and clinic type badge (e.g., “Public Health Centre”) as a rounded chip.
Location: Parish name with a map-pin icon.
Services: A horizontal, wrapping row of service chips listing everything the clinic offers.
Contact: Phone number as a clickable tel: link, and opening hours if available.
Actions: Two buttons — “Get Directions” (opens Google Maps) and “View on Map” (pans the Leaflet map to this clinic).
Use My Location & Get Directions
The “Use My Location” button is displayed prominently above the map:

On click, the browser’s permission prompt is triggered (navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition). If the user grants permission, a “You are here” marker (blue pulsing dot) is placed at the device’s GPS position.
Clinic cards are re-sorted by Haversine great-circle distance from the user’s position, so the nearest clinics float to the top of the list.

The “Get Directions” button on each card constructs a URL in the format https://www.google.com/maps/dir/?api=1&origin=LAT,LNG&destination=CLINIC_LAT,CLINIC_LNG&travelmode=driving and opens it in a new browser tab, launching Google Maps navigation.
9.1–9.4 UI Design Process

The Bloom user interface evolved through a structured, iterative design process: from rough paper sketches to wireframes to high-fidelity prototypes to a production implementation. Each stage was informed by feedback from peer reviews and usability observations, resulting in a final design that is both visually distinctive and highly functional.
9.1 Early Design — Wireframes

The initial design phase focused on information architecture and navigation structure before any visual styling decisions were made. Wireframes were produced as low-fidelity greyscale sketches for each of the four main screens.

Dashboard wireframe: Explored different card arrangements for the cycle summary. An early version placed trend charts at the top, but usability observations showed that users wanted to see their current cycle day first, before historical data. The layout was revised to lead with the Cycle Snapshot and Cycle Phase cards.

Calendar wireframe: The first version used a list view (similar to Google Calendar’s agenda view), but this made it difficult to see the overall pattern of a cycle at a glance. The wireframe was revised to a traditional monthly grid, which makes period and fertile-window blocks visually obvious.
Resource Centre wireframe: An early table-based layout was abandoned in favour of a card grid after comparing it to popular health content platforms, where card grids have proven higher engagement.

Clinic Finder wireframe: The initial wireframe placed the filter controls below the map, which testing showed was non-intuitive (users looked for filters before the map). The layout was revised to place filters above the map, matching the mental model users bring from travel and booking apps.

All wireframes were reviewed against the following principles: simple navigation structure, clear separation of features, and minimal visual clutter. Only elements that directly served a user task were included.
9.2 Design Iterations
Moving from wireframes to interactive prototypes, several significant design decisions were revised based on feedback:

Card-based layout adoption: The table-heavy early designs were replaced with a fully card-based layout across the Dashboard, Resources, and Clinic Finder. Cards proved more scannable and more naturally responsive on mobile.

Phase colour coding: The first prototype used a single pink accent for all cycle phases. Feedback highlighted that this made it impossible to distinguish phases at a glance on the calendar. Four distinct colours were introduced: deep red for menstruation, lavender for the follicular phase, green for ovulation, and warm amber for the luteal phase. Each colour was also assigned a text label and icon to support colour-blind users.

Cycle Log Modal redesign: The first version of the log form was a full page. Users found switching between the calendar and the log page disruptive. Moving the form into a modal overlay that slides up over the calendar solved this and was universally preferred in peer reviews.

Spacing and readability: Early prototypes had insufficient white space between UI elements, making the interface feel cramped. A 4 px base spacing scale was introduced and consistently applied, improving readability significantly, particularly on smaller screens.

Filter UX for the Clinic Finder: The original filter design used a sidebar panel that had to be explicitly opened. This was replaced with always-visible dropdown controls above the map, reducing the interaction cost of filtering from two taps to one.
9.3 Final UI Decisions
The final production design locked in the following key decisions:

Bloom Pink branding: The primary colour #C2187A was selected as the definitive Bloom brand colour after comparing multiple pink hues against accessibility contrast requirements. It achieves the required 4.5:1 contrast ratio against white at all text sizes.

Rounded component language: 8 px border-radius on cards and buttons, 16 px on modals. This softens the interface and communicates safety and approachability, which is especially important for a health application that may surface sensitive information.

Typography: Arial was selected as the primary typeface for its universal availability across operating systems, high legibility at small sizes, and neutral, professional character. Heading weights (700) create clear visual hierarchy without requiring a decorative display font.

Icon system: A consistent icon set (Heroicons outline style) is used for navigation items, action buttons, and category labels. Icons are always accompanied by a text label (never icon-only) on primary navigation elements, supporting users who cannot readily identify icons.

Micro-interactions: Subtle hover lifts (box-shadow increase + translateY(-2px)) on cards, smooth modal transitions (300 ms ease-out), and loading spinners on async actions were retained from the prototype stage as they significantly improved the perceived responsiveness of the application.
9.4 Navigation Flow
The final navigation architecture is intentionally shallow — every core feature is reachable within two taps from anywhere in the application:
The persistent top navigation bar provides direct links to Dashboard, Calendar, Resources, and Clinic Finder on all authenticated pages.
From the Dashboard, the user can reach the Calendar via the navigation bar or by clicking the Next Period date, which deep-links to the relevant calendar month.
From the Calendar, opening a day cell’s log entry and submitting updates the Dashboard in real time via Firestore listeners, creating a seamless loop between logging and insight.

From the Resource Centre, a “Find a Clinic” banner at the bottom of the page provides a contextual shortcut to the Clinic Finder, acknowledging that users reading health content may next want to seek in-person care.
The navigation flow was designed so that the most frequent user journey — log today’s data, check cycle phase, read a related resource — can be completed in under 3 minutes.
11.1 System Demo

The Bloom system demonstration presents a complete end-to-end walkthrough of the platform’s capabilities, showcasing how the frontend UI, Firebase backend, and external services work together to deliver a cohesive reproductive health tracking experience.
Demo Scenario: New User Onboarding to First Log
The demonstration follows a representative user — a 22-year-old Jamaican university student using Bloom for the first time — through the following sequence:

Registration: The user creates an account with email and password. Firebase Authentication creates the account and Firestore writes a new user profile document. The user is redirected to the Dashboard.
Dashboard first view: The Dashboard displays an empty cycle state with a prompt to add a first log. The Cycle Snapshot Card shows “No data yet — log your first cycle to get started”.
Opening the Cycle Log Modal: The user clicks the floating “+” button. The modal slides up. The date field defaults to today.
Logging data: The user selects “Heavy” flow, taps three symptom chips (cramps, fatigue, bloating), sets sleep score to 6, stress to 7, and adds a short note. Clicks Submit.

Real-time update: The modal closes. The Dashboard Cycle Snapshot Card immediately updates to show Day 1, phase “Menstruation”, and applies the red phase colour. The Calendar month view shows today’s cell highlighted with the period-day class.
Viewing the Resource Centre: The user navigates to Resources. Cards load from Firestore. The user filters by “Cycle Basics” and reads the “Understanding Your Menstrual Cycle” pamphlet.

Using the Clinic Finder: The user navigates to Clinic Finder, selects “St. Andrew” from the Parish filter and “Family Planning” from the Service filter. Three clinic cards appear and their markers are highlighted on the map. The user clicks “Get Directions” on the nearest clinic and is taken to Google Maps.
Demo Highlights
The demonstration specifically calls attention to:
The sub-second latency of Firestore real-time listeners updating the Dashboard after a log submission.
The accuracy of the cycle phase identification and next-period prediction after multiple logs are entered.
The responsiveness of the Clinic Finder map when filters are changed, with markers and cards updating simultaneously.
The seamless transition between mobile and desktop viewports, demonstrating that the application is fully usable on a smartphone.
11.4 UX Evaluation

A structured UX evaluation was conducted to assess whether Bloom’s interface meets its core usability goals. The evaluation combined peer usability observations, heuristic analysis against Nielsen’s 10 usability heuristics, and a review of task completion efficiency.
Navigation & Learnability

Evaluation finding: All five observed users located all four main features (Dashboard, Calendar, Resources, Clinic Finder) within 30 seconds of first encountering the application, without prompting. The persistent navigation bar and consistent page layout were credited as the primary contributors to this result.

Nielsen heuristic alignment: “Consistency and Standards” and “Recognition Rather Than Recall” are both met. Users could identify the purpose of each navigation item from its label and icon without needing to memorise the information architecture.
Minimal Learning Curve

Evaluation finding: First-time log entry (from opening the Cycle Log Modal to successfully submitting a log) was completed by all observed users in under 90 seconds, including reading the modal’s field labels. No user required assistance or produced an error state.

Nielsen heuristic alignment: “User Control and Freedom” is supported by the modal’s explicit Cancel button and Esc key dismissal. “Error Prevention” is addressed by validating only the one required field (flow intensity) and providing clear chip controls that eliminate free-text input errors for categorical data.
Visually Engaging Interface

Evaluation finding: All users commented positively on the interface’s visual design. Specific positive comments included the cycle phase colour coding (“I immediately knew what phase I was in because of the colour”), the circular progress ring on the Cycle Snapshot Card (“It’s like a fitness tracker, very satisfying”), and the overall pink branding (“It feels like it was made for me”).

These responses suggest that the design system decisions made in Section 9.3 — Bloom pink branding, rounded components, and phase colour coding — are well-aligned with the target user’s aesthetic preferences.
Practical and Relevant Insights

Evaluation finding: Users expressed high satisfaction with the Dashboard insights panel and cycle predictions. The plain-English phrasing of insights (“Your last 3 cycles have averaged 28 days”) was preferred over raw numerical displays. One user noted that seeing the predicted next period date on the Dashboard gave her “peace of mind” in a way that manual calendar tracking did not.
Areas for Future Improvement
The evaluation also identified several areas for future UX iteration:
Onboarding flow: New users with no log history see an empty Dashboard state. A guided onboarding wizard (prompting the user to enter their last period date) would accelerate time-to-first-insight.
Push notifications: Users expressed interest in receiving reminders before their predicted period or fertile window. A notification system (via Firebase Cloud Messaging) would address this.

Accessibility testing with assistive technology: While the interface was designed with WCAG 2.1 AA standards, a formal screen-reader audit (e.g., with NVDA or VoiceOver) has not yet been conducted and is recommended before wider public release.

Offline capability: Several users on mobile data connections experienced brief loading delays when switching between pages. A Progressive Web App (PWA) service worker caching strategy would improve performance on slower connections.

Appendix — Glossary
The following terms are used throughout the Bloom platform and its documentation.
Term
Definition
Cycle Phase

One of four recurring stages of the menstrual cycle: menstruation, follicular, ovulation, and luteal. Each phase is characterised by distinct hormonal patterns, physical symptoms, and emotional tendencies.
Fertile Window
The six-day period (five days before ovulation plus ovulation day) during which conception is biologically possible. Bloom estimates this window based on the predicted ovulation date.
Ovulation
The release of a mature egg (ovum) from the ovary, typically occurring around the midpoint of the menstrual cycle. Bloom estimates the ovulation day as 14 days before the predicted next period.
Cycle Prediction

An algorithmic estimate of future menstrual cycle events (period start date, ovulation date, fertile window) calculated from the rolling average of the user’s historical cycle lengths stored in Firestore.
Cycle Log
A daily health record created by the user via the Cycle Log Modal, capturing flow intensity, symptoms, sleep score, stress level, activity level, and free-text notes.
Cycle Length
The number of days from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Bloom tracks this for each cycle and uses the rolling average of the last six cycles for predictions.
Luteal Phase

The second half of the menstrual cycle, beginning after ovulation and ending at the start of the next period. Characterised by elevated progesterone levels and, in some users, premenstrual symptoms (PMS).
Follicular Phase
The first half of the menstrual cycle, beginning on the first day of menstruation and ending at ovulation. Oestrogen levels rise during this phase, leading to the development of ovarian follicles.
Flow Intensity
A categorical rating of menstrual flow volume: None, Spotting, Light, Medium, or Heavy. Logged daily by the user and used to identify period days on the calendar overlay.
Firestore
Cloud Firestore is Google’s scalable, NoSQL, document-oriented cloud database used by Bloom to store user profiles, cycle logs, educational resources, and clinic data in real time.
Leaflet.js
An open-source JavaScript library for interactive maps used in Bloom’s Clinic Finder to render the OpenStreetMap tile layer and display clinic location markers.
Haversine Distance

A mathematical formula used to calculate the great-circle distance between two points on the Earth’s surface given their latitude and longitude. Used by Bloom to sort clinic cards by proximity to the user’s location.
